12 genera and about 500 species in the Old and New World tropics, in some places extending to the subtropics, but absent from mainland Africa. In Peninsular Malaysia, represented by Elaeocarpus (36 species including a new unnamed species) and Sloanea (3 species).

Mostly in primary or secondary forest. Many species have scented flowers and nectar. Further east, in New Guinea and Australia, the fallen drupes of Elaeocarpus are eaten and dispersed by cassowaries and fruit pigeons; in the Peninsula, this role may be undertaken by monkeys and perhaps by large ground mammals.

Madagascar, Mauritius, India and Sri Lanka in the west to the Pacific in the east, from Japan in the north to New Zealand in the south. Of the 36 species recorded for Peninsular Malaysia, 19 species and 5 subspecies/varieties are endemic.

In forest from sea-level to upper montane forest, often in secondary forest, sometimes in swamp forest or occasionally estuarine habitats (E. macrocerus), (elsewhere in kerangas forest) but absent from mangroves. Characteristic of some species are their resinous terminal buds and often minutely toothed leaves that in many species turn red before they fall. They are readily recognised in flower by their pendent white fragrant flowers usually with laciniate petals, and in a few species by their blue fruits. The blue colour is not caused by pigmentation but by the structure of the cuticle that reflects blue light. The flowers are insect-pollinated, apparently involving two pollination syndromes: buzz pollination is characteristic of pendent flowers with short filaments, basifixed anthers with apical dehiscence and a punctiform stigma; while scented and nectiferous flowers will attract a different suite of pollinators (Coode, Fam. Gen. Vasc. Pl. 6 (2004) 135). The two types are exemplified by E. nitidus that is pollinated by the carpenter bees, Cerotina sp. and Braunsapis sp., and E. stipularis that are pollinated by bees, Apis sp. and Trigona sp. (Roubik et al., Pollination Ecology and the Rain Forest: Sarawak Studies (2006) 229). The bright blue fruits of E. angustifolius are dispersed in India by hornbills, flying squirrels, bats and gibbons (Khan et al. Current Science 88 (2005) 133--142). In southern Thailand, the bluish fruits of E. petiolatus are dispersed by the bushy-crested hornbill (Kitamura et al. Raffles Bull. Zool. Suppl. 24 (2011) 140). Norsham (FRIM Reports 83 (2005) 1--99) listed long-tailed macaques as consuming E. petiolatus fruits and the lar and agile gibbons as consuming fruits of an unidentified Elaeocarpus species. Tan et al. (J. Trop. Ecol. 14 (1998) 299--307) reported that the fruit bat Cynopterus brachyotis consumed the ?greenish fruits of E. stipularis.

Corner (1988) records that flowering is gregarious after marked dry weather, often at the beginning of the year. Flowers last a few days and are very fragrant (like Lily of the Valley).

The oily fruits are said to be edible and are eagerly consumed by monkeys (Gardner et al., 2011).

The three species in Peninsular Malaysia occupy separate habitats: Sloanea javanica is a lowland species, which occurs up to 300 m altitude, while S. malayana grows in hill forest between 600 and 670 m, and S. sigun in lower montane forest at about 1500 m.

Malesia: Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Java, Borneo (Brunei, Kalimantan and Sarawak), Sulawesi and the Philippines. In Peninsular Malaysia, not common, mostly in the south in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Selangor, also from Penang, Kelantan, Terengganu and Pahang.
